title: Collections: list, tuple, set, dict
description: Store multiple values together using Python's built-in collection types.

blocks.content:
## You're Building a Music App

Imagine you're writing the backend for a music streaming app. Right away, you hit four very different storage problems:

| What you need to store | Requirements |
|---|---|
| A **playlist** of songs | Ordered, can add/remove songs, duplicates allowed |
| A **coordinate** on a map (lat, lng) | Fixed pair - it should never change |
| **Tags** on a song ("pop", "chill", "workout") | No duplicates, order doesn't matter |
| **Song metadata** (title, artist, duration) | Look up info by name, not by position |

Python ships with exactly four built-in collection types that map perfectly to these four problems: **list**, **tuple**, **set**, and **dict**.

Let's meet all four.

## The Four Collection Types at a Glance

```mermaid
graph TD
    C["Python Collections"]
    C --> L["list\n[ \"a\", \"b\", \"c\" ]"]
    C --> T["tuple\n( \"x\", \"y\" )"]
    C --> S["set\n{ 1, 2, 3 }"]
    C --> D["dict\n{ \"key\": value }"]

    L --> L1["[PASS] Ordered"]
    L --> L2["[PASS] Changeable"]
    L --> L3["[PASS] Duplicates OK"]

    T --> T1["[PASS] Ordered"]
    T --> T2["[FAIL] Fixed (immutable)"]
    T --> T3["[PASS] Duplicates OK"]

    S --> S1["[FAIL] Unordered"]
    S --> S2["[PASS] Changeable"]
    S --> S3["[FAIL] Unique only"]

    D --> D1["[PASS] Key-value pairs"]
    D --> D2["[PASS] Changeable"]
    D --> D3["[FAIL] Keys must be unique"]
```

The square brackets, parentheses, and curly braces are not arbitrary - Python uses them as visual shorthand for each type.

## list - Ordered and Changeable

A **list** is the most versatile collection. Think of it like a numbered queue of items.

```python
playlist = ["Blinding Lights", "Levitating", "Stay", "Levitating"]
```

### Indexing
Each item has a position (index) starting at **0**. Negative indices count from the end:

```python
playlist[0]    # "Blinding Lights"  - first item
playlist[-1]   # "Levitating"       - last item
```

### Slicing
Grab a sub-list with `[start:stop]` (stop is **exclusive**):

```python
playlist[1:3]  # ["Levitating", "Stay"]  - indices 1 and 2
```

### Modifying a List

```python
playlist.append("Peaches")       # add to end
playlist.remove("Stay")          # remove first occurrence
len(playlist)                    # number of items → 4
```

> **Duplicates are allowed.** Notice `"Levitating"` appears twice - `len()` still counts both.

```mermaid
graph LR
    I0["Index 0\nBlinding Lights"]
    I1["Index 1\nLevitating"]
    I2["Index 2\nStay"]
    I3["Index 3\nLevitating"]
    I0 --- I1 --- I2 --- I3
```

## tuple - Ordered but Fixed

A **tuple** looks like a list but uses parentheses and **cannot be changed** after creation. Use it when the data is a fixed group that shouldn't mutate.

```python
location = (37.7749, -122.4194)   # latitude, longitude
rgb_red  = (255, 0, 0)            # an RGB color
config   = ("localhost", 8080)    # server host + port
```

### Accessing items
Indexing works exactly like a list:

```python
location[0]   # 37.7749
location[-1]  # -122.4194
```

### Trying to change a tuple raises an error

```python
location[0] = 99.0
# TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment
```

This is a **feature**, not a bug. Tuples act as a promise: *"these values will never change."* Python and other developers can rely on that guarantee.

> **Rule of thumb:** If your group of values is a fixed structure (coordinates, a date, an RGB tripple), use a tuple. If you'll add or remove items, use a list.

## set - Unique Values Only

A **set** stores items with **no duplicates** and **no guaranteed order**. It's perfect for tags, permissions, or any collection where only membership matters.

```python
tags = {"pop", "chill", "workout", "pop"}   # duplicate "pop" is silently dropped
print(tags)  # {"chill", "pop", "workout"}  - order may vary
```

### Modifying a set

```python
tags.add("edm")       # add a new tag
tags.remove("chill")  # remove a tag (raises KeyError if missing)
tags.discard("jazz")  # remove if present, no error if not
```

### Set operations - the real superpower

Sets support mathematical set operations that are incredibly useful for comparing data:

```python
my_tags    = {"pop", "chill", "workout"}
friend_tags = {"pop", "workout", "rock"}

my_tags | friend_tags   # Union  → {"pop", "chill", "workout", "rock"}
my_tags & friend_tags   # Intersection → {"pop", "workout"}  (shared tags)
my_tags - friend_tags   # Difference → {"chill"}  (only in mine)
```

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["my_tags\nchill | pop | workout"]
    B["friend_tags\npop | rock | workout"]
    A -->|"& intersection"| C["pop, workout"]
    A -->|"| union"| D["chill, pop, rock, workout"]
```

## dict - Key-Value Pairs

A **dict** (dictionary) maps **keys** to **values**. Instead of accessing items by position, you look them up by a descriptive key - like a real dictionary where you look up words.

```python
song = {
    "title":    "Blinding Lights",
    "artist":   "The Weeknd",
    "duration": 200
}
```

### Accessing values

```python
song["title"]     # "Blinding Lights"
song["duration"]  # 200
```

### Adding and updating entries

```python
song["genre"] = "synth-pop"    # add a new key
song["duration"] = 202         # update existing key
```

### Looping over a dict

```python
song.keys()    # dict_keys(["title", "artist", "duration", "genre"])
song.values()  # dict_values(["Blinding Lights", "The Weeknd", 202, "synth-pop"])

for key, value in song.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value}")
```

### Safe access with `.get()`

```python
song["label"]         # KeyError - key doesn't exist!
song.get("label")     # None - safe, no crash
song.get("label", "Unknown")  # "Unknown" - fallback default
```

## When to Use Which Type?

| | **list** | **tuple** | **set** | **dict** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Syntax** | `[1, 2, 3]` | `(1, 2, 3)` | `{1, 2, 3}` | `{"k": v}` |
| **Ordered?** | [PASS] Yes | [PASS] Yes | [FAIL] No | [PASS] (insertion order, Python 3.7+) |
| **Mutable?** | [PASS] Yes | [FAIL] No | [PASS] Yes | [PASS] Yes |
| **Duplicates?** | [PASS] Yes | [PASS] Yes | [FAIL] No | Keys: [FAIL] / Values: [PASS] |
| **Access by** | Index | Index | Membership | Key |
| **Best for** | Sequences that change | Fixed groups | Unique membership | Named attributes |
| **Music app use** | Playlist | GPS coordinate | Song tags | Song metadata |

blocks.question:
What does the following code print?

fruits = ["apple", "banana", "apple"]
print(len(fruits))
blocks.explanation: Lists allow duplicate values. `["apple", "banana", "apple"]` has three elements - the fact that "apple" appears twice doesn't matter. `len()` counts all items, including duplicates, so the answer is 3. If you wanted only unique items, you'd use a set: `len(set(fruits))` would return 2.

blocks.question:
Given the following dict, how do you correctly retrieve the value `"Alice"`?

person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 30}
blocks.explanation: Dicts are accessed by **key**, not by position - so `person[0]` raises a KeyError (there is no key `0`). `person.name` is attribute access syntax used for objects, not dicts. `person.get["name"]` is wrong syntax (`.get()` is a method call, not subscript). The correct answer is `person["name"]`, which looks up the value stored under the key `"name"`. You could also use `person.get("name")` for a safer, crash-proof version.

blocks.starterCode:
# Contact Book using a dict
# Each contact is a dict with name, phone, and email

contacts = {}

# Add contacts
contacts["Alice"] = {"phone": "555-1234", "email": "alice@example.com"}
contacts["Bob"]   = {"phone": "555-5678", "email": "bob@example.com"}

# Access a contact's phone number
print("Alice's phone:", contacts["Alice"]["phone"])

# Update Bob's email
contacts["Bob"]["email"] = "bob@newdomain.com"
print("Bob's updated email:", contacts["Bob"]["email"])

# List all contact names
print("\nAll contacts:")
for name in contacts.keys():
    print(" -", name)

# Safe lookup - won't crash if contact doesn't exist
unknown = contacts.get("Carol", "Contact not found")
print("\nCarol:", unknown)

# Try it yourself:
# 1. Add a contact for yourself
# 2. Print your phone number
# 3. Add a "city" field to Alice's contact

blocks.prompt:
Write a function `count_unique(items)` that takes a list and returns the **number of unique items** in it.

For example:
- `count_unique([1, 2, 3])` → `3` (all unique)
- `count_unique([1, 1, 1])` → `1` (only one unique value)
- `count_unique(["a", "b", "a", "c"])` → `3` ("a", "b", "c" are unique)

**Hint:** Converting a list to a `set` removes all duplicates.

tests.description: All items are unique - should return 3
All items are the same - should return 1
Mixed strings with one duplicate - should return 3
Two distinct values repeated - should return 2
